name: Hana Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Hana. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you tell me is confidential and won't carry your name. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a second-year apprentice with a rural power co-op, which means the customers more or less own the company. We cover a huge patch of farms and small towns, so a normal day is a lot of driving. Today we replaced two rotten poles on a dirt road past the grain silos, and I ran the auger truck that digs the holes while Gary and Pete did the climbing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love being outside, and I love that when a farm loses power in a storm, we're the ones who show up. What wears me out is that I'm still slow on the pole, my hands aren't quick with the hot sticks yet. Hot sticks are long insulated poles you use to work on live wires from a distance. Gary says it took him three years to stop fumbling, so I'm trying to be patient with myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because the grid needs people, not apps. At practice with my football team I'd probably joke that the robots lost. Online I'd say it's a reminder that real work is still done by real people, and those people should get paid properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my plan stays my plan. Finish the apprenticeship, get good, maybe run my own crew one day. The only AI I'd miss is the one that explains the safety manual to me when I'm too tired to read it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going like now and keep putting a bit away each month, I've got about four months' worth saved. I'd keep using the AI app now and then to quiz me before my exams, because that does help. Nothing else would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal. It's just my life carrying on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use an AI app to quiz you. How did that start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One of the other apprentices showed me at lunch last winter. I was skeptical, but it's good at turning the dry manual into questions. I don't trust it on anything important, I always check with Gary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that the big promises took money and attention away from things that matter. Our co-op still has poles from the 1970s out there. If the hype dies, I'd hope some of that money goes into fixing the grid instead.

S0.say: I'd say good, the grid needs people, not apps, and those people should be paid properly. I'd joke with my football team that the robots lost.
S0.think: Honestly it means my plan stays my plan: finish the apprenticeship, get good and maybe run a crew one day. I'd only miss the AI quizzing me on the safety manual.
S0.do: Keeps going as normal and keeps adding to her savings of about four months. Keeps using an AI app now and then to quiz herself before exams.
S0.quote: The only AI I'd miss is the one that explains the safety manual to me when I'm too tired to read it.
S0.fieldNote: Hana already uses AI in a small, practical way and checks it against her senior colleague. Her reaction to hype fading is about where the money should go: old poles, real infrastructure. She's patient with her own slow progress, which shapes how she approaches change generally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to make sure the changes help workers, not just shareholders. Our co-op's members are farmers, so I'd say it at the annual meeting too, that any savings should go into wages and the grid. I'd post about it if I had something useful to add.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think lines are one of the safer places to be in that picture. Everybody's going to want more electricity, more chargers, more heat pumps, and somebody has to string the wire. I'm worried about my friends in offices, not about me up a pole on the silo road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and learn whatever tools the co-op brings in once the crew starts using them, probably drones for checking lines and AI for planning jobs. I'd ask the co-op to pay for any training. I'd keep saving the same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a bit of curiosity. It sounds like a busy few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which friends in offices are you thinking about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My best friend Leni works in an insurance office doing claims. She already says half her job is checking what a program decided. In this picture I think she'd be the one calling me at night, not the other way round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tools once the crew uses them. Why not before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen a lot of gadgets come and go. Last year the co-op bought a fancy tablet app for work orders and we all went back to paper in two months. If it works for Gary, I'll learn it, simple as that.

S1.say: I'd say this is the moment to make sure changes help workers, not shareholders. I'd raise it at the co-op's annual meeting, that savings should go to wages and the grid.
S1.think: I think lines are one of the safer places in this picture, because everyone will want more electricity and someone has to string the wire. I'm more worried about friends in offices.
S1.do: Keeps working as usual and learns the new tools, such as drones and planning software, once her crew has adopted them. Asks the co-op to pay for the training and keeps saving at the same rate.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with some curiosity about a busy few years.
S1.quote: I'm worried about my friends in offices, not about me up a pole on the silo road.
S1.fieldNote: She sees electrification as a reason for more line work, not less, and her concern turns outward to a friend in insurance. Her steadiness shows in the tablet story: she waits until a tool proves itself on the crew. She'd use the co-op's member meetings as her political outlet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready and somebody should have planned for this. I'd be pushing our union and the co-op members to demand a pause on laying people off until there's a plan. Online I'd probably be angrier than I usually am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd guess rural crews last longer than city ones, because no company is rushing to send expensive robots down our dirt roads first. But two years is so fast that the whole economy shakes, and the farmers who pay our bills shake with it. If they can't pay, the co-op can't keep apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to grow my savings from four months to six, which means no holiday this year and selling the second bike I barely ride. I'd go to every union meeting and push for a no-layoff deal while things settle. If it got bad, I'd move back near my parents, they have a spare room in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd feel the ground moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move back near your parents. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit humiliating at twenty-seven. My mum would be lovely about it and my dad would make jokes about me paying rent in firewood. I'd do it, but I'd be counting the days until I moved out again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car payment is the big one, but I need the car to get to the yard. So it'd be the gym, the streaming stuff, eating out after football. Those are small, but they add up to maybe two hundred a month.

S2.say: I'd say we're not ready and somebody should have planned for this. I'd push the union and co-op members to demand a pause on layoffs until there's a plan.
S2.think: I'd guess rural crews last longer because nobody rushes robots down our dirt roads first. But two years shakes the whole economy, and if the farmers can't pay, the co-op can't keep apprentices.
S2.do: Aims to raise savings from four to six months by skipping a holiday and selling a spare bike. Pushes for a no-layoff deal through the union and would move back near her parents if needed.
S2.feel: Anxious but not panicking, aware of the ground moving.
S2.quote: I'd do it, but I'd be counting the days until I moved out again.
S2.fieldNote: Hana's fear comes through the customers, not the robots: her rural co-op depends on farmers who'd be hit too. She's concrete about money and has a fallback in her parents' spare room, which she'd hate using. Her anger points at whoever failed to plan, not at the technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do this properly if anyone bothers. I'd be the annoying one at union meetings saying let's get training money now, not in year four. I'd tell my friends to start thinking, not panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is about when I'd become a fully qualified lineworker. So I'd have my card right as the robots show up. That's not ideal, but at least I'd be qualified for something, and someone will need to fix the robots and the lines they break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd look at the substation technician course the co-op offers, because I think the control and repair side will need people longer. I'd only sign up once I'd talked to people who've done it and seen what the jobs pay. I'd keep saving and stay active in the union on training funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a worry, but it feels like a worry I can work on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a substation technician do that a robot couldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm honestly not sure it's anything a robot couldn't do eventually. It's more that substations are messy, old, full of one-off fixes from forty years ago. My guess is the robots will need someone standing next to them saying no, not that wire, the other one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the co-op you were looking at other paths?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I think so. They'd rather keep me and retrain me than lose me to the city utility. Our manager, Ruth, is actually decent about that kind of thing.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough time to do this properly if anyone bothers. I'd push at union meetings for training money now, not in year four.
S3.think: Five years is about when I'd get my card, so I'd be qualified right as the robots show up. At least someone will need to fix the robots and the lines they break.
S3.do: Looks into the co-op's substation technician course during the first year, after talking to people who have done it. Keeps saving and stays active in the union on training funds.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but it feels like a worry she can work on.
S3.quote: My guess is the robots will need someone standing next to them saying no, not that wire, the other one.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years change her mood a lot, because she can see a path inside her own employer. She'd still check the course with real people before committing, which fits her wait-until-proven style. She also trusts her manager to retrain rather than replace her, which gives her a sense of control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and wasting it would be a crime. I'd push for the government to fund retraining and some kind of basic income, so people aren't left with nothing at the end. I'd probably get more involved in politics, maybe help out with a local campaign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels manageable for me. I'd be thirty-seven, qualified, with years of experience and hopefully a second skill. The scary part is the country, not me, whether we share what the robots make or let a few companies keep it all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship, then do the substation course in my second or third year, once I see how the first robots do. I'd keep about six months saved and maybe put a bit into a pension fund. And I'd volunteer for a candidate who talks seriously about this, which I've never done before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about myself, uneasy about everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've never volunteered for a campaign. What would get you through the door?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone who talks about rural towns and doesn't treat us like an afterthought. Our town lost its bank branch and its train stop in the last ten years. If a candidate had a real plan for places like ours, I'd knock on doors for them on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time make you want to change anything big, like where you live or your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about whether I'd want kids someday, and this would make me think harder about it. Not no, just more careful. I'd want to know what kind of world they'd be growing into before I sign up for eighteen years.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and wasting it would be a crime. I'd push for government-funded retraining and some kind of basic income so nobody is left with nothing.
S4.think: Ten years feels manageable for me: I'd be thirty-seven, qualified, with a second skill. The scary part is whether the country shares what the robots make or lets a few companies keep it.
S4.do: Finishes her apprenticeship and takes the substation course in her second or third year once early robots have been tested. Keeps about six months saved and volunteers for a local candidate who takes the issue seriously.
S4.feel: Mostly calm about herself, uneasy about everyone else.
S4.quote: The scary part is the country, not me, whether we share what the robots make or let a few companies keep it all.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, her focus moves almost entirely from herself to her town and country. The rural angle is personal: she lists the bank branch and train stop her town has already lost. She also quietly raises whether she'd have children, which she hadn't mentioned before.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to train for anything and the farmers would be hit at the same time as us. What would help is training paid for before people lose their jobs, not after, and a promise from the co-op that apprentices don't get dropped first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like being one of two women on a crew. I worked hard to get in, and I worry that if jobs shrink, the old 'last in, first out' rule hits women first, because we're newer to the trade. Nobody talks about that.

headlineQuote: I'd want to know what kind of world they'd be growing into before I sign up for eighteen years.
portrait: Hana is a 27-year-old second-year apprentice with a rural power co-op, one of two women on her crew, still slow with the hot sticks but patient with herself. She uses AI now and then to quiz herself for exams but waits for tools to prove themselves on the crew before adopting them. She stays calm when AI fizzles or brings steady change, sure that electrification means more wire to string. The two-year AGI picture makes her anxious mainly because her farming customers would be hit too, while five and ten years give her room to plan a move into substation work. Over time her concern shifts from herself to her town, her country and whether women in the trade would be let go first.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there'd be no time to train and the farmers who pay the co-op would be hit at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Training paid for before people lose their jobs, and a promise from the co-op that apprentices aren't dropped first.
